reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma
clinicalPearls: An inflammatory disorder of one or more extraocular muscles, usually considered a myositic subtype of idiopathic orbital inflammation
Typical presentation is with acute painful diplopia, pain worsened by eye movement, redness over the involved muscle insertion, and restricted motility
It is frequently unilateral and often affects a single muscle, most commonly a horizontal rectus
On orbital imaging the affected muscle is enlarged with characteristic involvement of the tendon, in contrast to the tendon-sparing enlargement of thyroid eye disease
Injection and swelling are often most marked over the insertion of the inflamed muscle
Most cases respond briskly to systemic corticosteroids, with relief of pain and improvement in movement, though recurrence can occur
Atypical, recurrent, bilateral, or treatment-resistant cases warrant investigation and sometimes biopsy to exclude specific inflammations, IgG4-related disease, vasculitis, and lymphoma
The key clinical distinction from thyroid eye disease is the pain, tendon involvement, and usually single-muscle pattern
reference.pathophysiology: Orbital myositis is inflammation localised to the extraocular muscles, with an infiltrate of lymphocytes and other inflammatory cells causing the muscle belly and, characteristically, its tendon of insertion to swell. The inflamed, oedematous muscle contracts and moves poorly, producing pain on eye movement, diplopia, and restriction, while overlying congestion causes redness at the insertion. It is regarded as a form of idiopathic orbital inflammation confined to muscle, and some cases fall within the IgG4-related disease spectrum or accompany systemic inflammatory disorders. The immune-mediated nature explains the typically rapid response to corticosteroids, whereas persistent or recurrent inflammation can lead to fibrosis with fixed restriction.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic orbital inflammation of other patterns
Orbital metastasis or lymphoma involving muscle
Systemic vasculitis or IgG4-related orbital disease
additionalInvestigations: Orbital CT or MRI demonstrating enlargement of the affected muscle with tendon involvement
Assessment of ocular motility, diplopia, and pain on eye movement
Visual acuity, colour vision, and pupil assessment to exclude optic-nerve involvement
Bloods including inflammatory markers, thyroid function and autoantibodies, and serum IgG4 to exclude mimics
ANCA and systemic workup where vasculitis or systemic disease is suspected
Biopsy in atypical, recurrent, or steroid-unresponsive cases
redFlags: Poor or absent response to corticosteroids suggesting an alternative diagnosis such as lymphoma
Bilateral or recurrent myositis pointing to a systemic or IgG4-related cause
Signs of optic-nerve compromise or marked proptosis
Features suggesting infection or a carotid-cavernous fistula rather than sterile inflammation
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally good, with most single-muscle cases responding promptly to corticosteroids, but recurrences are common and repeated or chronic inflammation may cause muscle fibrosis with persistent diplopia and restriction needing further treatment.
pitfalls: Confusing it with thyroid eye disease by overlooking the pain and tendon involvement
Mistaking it for orbital cellulitis and treating with antibiotics alone
Attributing a poor steroid response to underdosing rather than reconsidering the diagnosis
Failing to investigate recurrent or bilateral disease for a systemic cause
Missing IgG4-related disease or vasculitis underlying the myositis
management: Use systemic corticosteroids as the mainstay, which usually produce brisk relief of pain and restriction
Consider NSAIDs alone for mild, isolated disease
Add steroid-sparing immunosuppression (methotrexate, mycophenolate) or biologic therapy for recurrent, steroid-dependent or refractory cases
Reserve low-dose orbital radiotherapy for disease refractory to immunosuppression
Confirm the diagnosis with orbital imaging and exclude mimics such as thyroid eye disease and IgG4-related disease before committing to long-term therapy
Monitor for recurrence and fibrosis, and manage residual diplopia with prisms or strabismus surgery once stable
